_doc: Single source for SD-03's technology choices. Read by video/src/stack.py, which feeds the 5.1 technology slides, the stack table, the fix-slide 'Rejected' lines and the C4 technology labels (video/diagrams.py), and rewrites the marked regions of the booklet (Stage 5) and OUTLINE.md. Edit here, then run video/src/stack.py sync (build-video.sh and build-sd-booklet.sh do it). Text is Markdown-lite: `code` and **bold** only. A slide's `how` is two or three sentences; the rest goes in `detail` (booklet only). The compact cut has no drill interlude, so no entry carries a slide drill; the booklet keeps the probes in `drill`.

stack.heading: Collector: a stateless Go service with a disk spool
stack.title: A stateless collector that says yes only when the log has it
stack.pick: Go on Kubernetes, behind an L4 load balancer
stack.why: It does three things and nothing else: validate, stamp the server time, append. Stateless, so it scales on CPU; the ack means durable.
stack.how: Batches of up to 500 events, produced to Kafka with `acks=all` and the idempotent producer; `202` only after the ack. If Kafka is unreachable: a bounded disk spool for ten minutes, then `503`.
stack.detail: The collector never generates an event ID and never deduplicates: the ID is minted by the SDK or the ad server when the event happens, and dedup is downstream. It adds `server_ts` and the collector ID. Client time is kept as `client_ts`; the event time is the client time when it lies within 72 hours before and 5 minutes after the server time, and the server time otherwise, with a `clamped` flag. Producer settings: `linger.ms=20`, `batch.size` 256 KB, zstd compression, `enable.idempotence=true`. The spool is an append-only file per pod, replayed in order on reconnect; a pod that dies with a non-empty spool is drained by its replacement from the same persistent volume.
rejected: Warehouse streaming inserts
Ties ingest to the store's quotas, and leaves no replayable log.
Access logs shipped by an agent
The client hears yes before the event is durable.
summary: the ack means the log has it
stack.course: building-blocks course, part 11 §11.10 (idempotent writes) and part 12 §12.5 (load shedding)
drill: Kafka is down for four minutes. What do the SDKs and the collectors do?

The collector spools to local disk and keeps answering 202 for up to ten minutes; past that it answers 503 and the SDK keeps its own buffer and retries with the same event IDs. Nothing acknowledged is lost; duplicates from the retries are removed downstream.
spool, then 503; the SDK keeps the IDs; dedup downstream

stack.heading: Event log: Kafka, keyed by event ID
stack.title: Kafka: 1,024 partitions, keyed by event ID, three days on the brokers
stack.why: A replayable log is the one copy everything is derived from; keyed by event ID, load is even and a retry lands beside its original.
stack.how: Topic `events.raw`: partition = hash(event ID) mod 1,024, RF 3 over three zones, `min.insync.replicas=2`. Brokers keep three days.
stack.detail: Brokers keep three days (about 390 TB compressed, with replicas); replays older than that read the lake. Keying by ad would put a 2-million-a-second ad on one partition; keying by event ID spreads it and keeps a retry on the same partition as its original, which the stream's dedup uses. Six gigabytes a second at peak, three replicas, is 18 GB/s of broker writes: about 80 brokers at 250 MB/s each (illustrative). Consumer groups: the live aggregator, the lake sink. Tiered storage is possible but not relied on. RabbitMQ was also rejected: a queue, not a log, so a consumed message is gone and there is nothing to replay.
rejected: Google Pub/Sub
An honest equal on Google Cloud; rejected for per-key placement and portability.
Amazon Kinesis
1 MB/s a shard: about 6,000 shards to manage at 6 GB/s.
stack.course: building-blocks course, part 10 §10.2–10.5 (inside a partitioned log, delivery semantics)

stack.heading: Live aggregator: Flink, streaming
stack.title: Flink: deduplicate, combine, then count by event time
stack.why: Keyed state with a TTL, event-time windows, and checkpoints that hold state and offsets together. The same job runs in batch mode for the bill.
stack.how: Dedup keyed by event ID (TTL 10 min), a per-subtask combiner flushed every second, then ad × minute windows: early results every 2 s, final on the watermark. Checkpoints every 30 s.
stack.detail: The watermark is the minimum over partitions of (largest event time seen minus 2 minutes); an idle partition is excluded after 30 seconds so it cannot hold the watermark back. Allowed lateness is one hour: a late event updates its minute again; anything later goes to a side output that only counts late events (the lake has them anyway). Unique reach is a HyperLogLog sketch per campaign and minute, merged across minutes on read. The sink writes rows with a version (window end, emit sequence) so a re-emitted minute replaces the old row. Dataflow (Apache Beam) is an honest equal on Google Cloud: the same model as a service; rejected only to keep one engine for both runs on any cloud.
rejected: Kafka Streams
Re-keying to the ad writes a repartition topic: another 6 GB/s through the brokers.
Spark Structured Streaming
A near-equal; micro-batches eat into the 10 s budget.
summary: state TTL, watermarks, one engine for both runs
stack.course: building-blocks course, part 10 §10.11–10.13 (event time, stateful processing, Lambda and Kappa)
drill: Your watermark stops moving. What happened, and what do the dashboards show?

Usually one idle or stuck partition: the watermark is a minimum. Idle partitions are excluded after 30 seconds; a stuck one shows as lag on that partition. Early firings keep the dashboard moving, marked provisional, while on-time results wait.
a minimum over partitions; idle timeout; early firings

stack.heading: Live store: ClickHouse, replacing by version
stack.title: ClickHouse: minute rows that are replaced, never incremented
stack.why: Columnar scans answer a dashboard in milliseconds; a row keyed by what it counts, with a version, makes a re-emitted minute a replacement.
stack.how: `live_minute ORDER BY (campaign_id, ad_id, minute, shard)` with a `version` column, inserted in batches. Reads take the latest version per key and sum the shards.
stack.detail: Sharded across nodes by campaign so one advertiser's dashboard hits one shard. A hot ad writes up to 16 rows a minute (one per combiner shard); the read sums them. Merges collapse replaced rows in the background; until then `argMax` by version (or `FINAL` on small ranges) gives the right answer. Closed hours are also loaded from the billing tables into `final_hour`, so one query serves both. Bigtable was also rejected: fast row reads, but no aggregation queries, so every dashboard becomes a scan in the API.
rejected: Apache Druid / Pinot
Honest equals; more moving parts for no property we need.
Redis counters
An increment is not replay-safe, and history does not fit in memory.
stack.course: building-blocks course, part 14 §14.9 (columnar storage) and part 8 §8.10 (split counters)

stack.heading: Event lake and billing tables: Iceberg on object storage
stack.title: Iceberg tables: snapshots to pin, partitions to overwrite
stack.pick: Apache Iceberg on GCS, Parquet + zstd
stack.why: Each commit is a snapshot with an ID, so a run pins what it read, and replacing an hour is atomic.
stack.how: `events` partitioned by event hour, 0.6 PB a month. `billing_hour` keyed by (campaign, ad, hour, version); each run commits version n + 1 with its manifest.
stack.detail: The lake sink (a Flink job) commits files every five minutes; late events for an old hour are new files in that hour's partition, stamped with the ingest time, so "hour H as of the cutoff" is a snapshot, not a guess. Raw events are kept six months (the dispute window is 90 days) and then expired by snapshot expiry; billing tables are kept seven years (about 15 TB). The billing job is the live aggregator's code run in Flink's batch mode over one hour: the same dedup, combine and window operators, with all data present. BigQuery as the system of record was also considered: a good choice on Google Cloud, rejected here for the per-query cost of re-running months and to keep the truth in open files.
rejected: Plain Parquet folders
No atomic overwrite and no snapshot: a reader can see half an hour.
Delta Lake
An honest equal; Iceberg chosen for engine-neutral tables.
stack.course: building-blocks course, part 7 §7.7 (multi-version storage) and part 10 §10.13 (batch and stream)
drill: Finance wants last March re-run and bit-identical. What makes that possible?

The March manifests: each names the Iceberg snapshot of the events, the rate-card version, the invalidation-list snapshot and the job's image digest. Re-running that image over those snapshots gives the same rows, because the job uses no wall clock, sums integers, and sorts before it reduces.
pinned snapshot, rate card, invalidations, image digest

1: it removes a producer's own retry inside one session; an SDK retry over HTTP is a new request, and only dedup on the event ID removes it.
2: they bill a phone's Tuesday-evening impressions in Wednesday's 6 a.m. hour.
3: one key is one shard's thread, about 100,000 operations a second against 2 million, and a replay increments again.
4: it makes one run's output atomic; a second run from four hours earlier still adds on top unless the write replaces by key.
5: the invoice then matches no stored version, and the audit trail ends at the edit.
6: they stay green while the pipeline counts wrong; only conservation checks and canaries see a wrong number.
